\title{Counting Collapse: A Formally Verified Attractor Theory of\\
       Repetition Hallucination in Autoregressive Text-to-Speech}

\twoauthors
  {Ivan Viakhirev$^{1}$, Kirill Borodin$^{2,3}$, Grach Mkrtchian$^{2}$}

\begin{abstract}
Autoregressive text-to-speech models loop, truncate, and lose count on text that
repeats a phrase many times. We show this is not a sampling accident but a
structural limit. Modelling one repetition as a state map $F$ on the decoder's
hidden state, we prove that if $F$ contracts with factor $q<1$ then \emph{no}
Lipschitz readout---the model's own stop head included---can separate repetition
counts beyond a horizon $N^\ast \le \log(\mu/2LC)/\log q$. The theorem and a
companion attention-dilution lemma are machine-checked in Lean~4 with
\texttt{mathlib}, free of \texttt{sorry} and of nonstandard axioms. Across
\NModels{} checkpoints from \NFamilies{} families, judged by a CTC recogniser
because the obvious autoregressive judge is itself biased against repetition,
models render repeated text with a median count error of \ErrRep{}\% at $k\ge6$
while length-matched sequences of \emph{distinct} words come out exact
(\ErrCtl{}\%) at every $k$ up to $32$: the limit tracks periodicity, not length.
The theorem's consequence is directly observable --- the number of
distinguishable states a generation visits grows with $k$ at a factor
\CapRatio{} of the control rate, with disjoint bootstrap intervals in all six
--- and survives controls for output monotony. The decoder does not merely err on
repeated text; it runs out of states in which the count could be represented.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
speech synthesis, hallucination, autoregressive models, formal verification,
fixed-point dynamics
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Ask an autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) model to say \emph{six hundred
sixty-six thousand six hundred sixty-six}, or to repeat a word a dozen times,
and it will frequently get the count wrong: it stops early, runs on, or locks
into a loop. The behaviour is well documented as a stability
problem~\cite{wang2025eliminating,song2024ellav}, and is usually attributed to
exposure bias or to the absence of a monotonic alignment constraint, with fixes
proposed at the level of attention supervision or decoding
rules~\cite{xin2024ralle,du2024cosyvoice2}.

We argue that a large part of this behaviour has a simpler and more fundamental
cause, and that the cause can be stated as a theorem. When the conditioning text
contains $k$ copies of the same phrase, softmax attention over those copies
cannot tell one copy from another: each receives weight $\Theta(1/k)$ and the
attention profile flattens (Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution}). The decoder therefore
receives approximately the \emph{same} conditioning at every repetition
boundary, so the map carrying it from one boundary to the next is approximately
autonomous. If that map contracts, the decoder's internal record of how many
repetitions it has produced is erased at a geometric rate, and past a computable
horizon no Lipschitz function of the state---the stop-token logit
included---can recover the count (Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}). Looping and
truncation are then the only behaviours available.

The failure is thus predicted to depend on \emph{periodicity}, not on length: a
sequence of $k$ distinct words should survive where $k$ identical ones do not.
That contrast is the sharpest empirical test we run, and models pass and fail it
exactly as predicted.

We contribute a quantitative impossibility result for repetition counting in AR
decoders, with an explicit horizon in terms of the contraction factor, the orbit
scale and the readout's decision margin; a machine-checked proof of it, and of
the attention-dilution lemma, in Lean~4 over \texttt{mathlib} with a reproducible
axiom audit --- to our knowledge the first hallucination result in speech
synthesis carried out as a formal artifact; and a parametric repetition-ladder
benchmark with a measurement protocol that reads the theorem's own consequence
off a model's activations. The work is the autoregressive-decoder companion to a
spectral study of hallucination in encoder--decoder
ASR~\cite{viakhirev2026dispersion}, which identified an attractor regime
descriptively; here the attractor is what the theorem is about.

\section{Counting Collapse}
\label{sec:theory}

Let $S$ be the decoder state space, a nonempty complete metric space ($\mathbb{R}^d$
in practice). Fix a prompt containing $k$ copies of a phrase and write
$s_m \in S$ for the state at the $m$-th \emph{repetition boundary}, after $m$
copies have been rendered.

\begin{assumption}[Periodic conditioning]\label{ass:periodic}
There is a single map $F : S \to S$ with $s_{m+1} = F(s_m)$ for all $m$.
\end{assumption}

This is what the following lemma buys: if the decoder cannot distinguish the $k$
text spans, the update it applies between consecutive boundaries is the same to
within $O(\delta + 1/k)$.

\begin{lemma}[Attention dilution]\label{lem:dilution}
Let $z_1,\dots,z_k$ be attention logits over the $k$ repeated spans with
$z_a - z_b \le \delta$ for all $a,b$. Then
$e^{-\delta}/k \le \mathrm{softmax}(z)_i \le e^{\delta}/k$ for every $i$, hence
$|\mathrm{softmax}(z)_i - \mathrm{softmax}(z)_j| \le (e^\delta-e^{-\delta})/k$,
and the profile entropy satisfies $H \ge \log k - \delta$.
\end{lemma}

The profile is within $O(1/k)$ of uniform: attention weight carries vanishing
information about \emph{which} occurrence is being rendered.

\begin{assumption}[Contraction]\label{ass:contraction}
$F$ is $q$-Lipschitz with $q < 1$.
\end{assumption}

Assumption~\ref{ass:contraction} is an empirical claim about a particular
decoder, not something we prove about transformers; where it fails, the theorem
is silent, and we report that as a distinct regime rather than a failed
prediction. Write $C = d(s_0, F s_0)/(1-q)$ for the orbit scale.

\begin{theorem}[Counting collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:periodic} and~\ref{ass:contraction}: (i)
$d(s_m, s^\ast) \le C q^m$ for the unique fixed point $s^\ast$; (ii) for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(s_m,s_n)<\varepsilon$ for all $m,n \ge N$;
(iii) every $L$-Lipschitz readout $g$ satisfies
$|g(s_m)-g(s_n)| \le LC(q^m+q^n)$; and therefore (iv) if $g$ still separates
counts $m \le n$ with decision margin $\mu>0$, then $\mu \le 2LCq^m$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:horizon}
  m \;\le\; \log\!\big(\mu / (2LC)\big)\big/\log q \;=:\; N^\ast .
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

Part~(iv) is the operative statement: the number of repetitions an AR decoder can
count is bounded by how fast its per-repetition map contracts, how large its
orbit is, and how much separation its readout needs. No property of the decoding
rule enters, so the bound applies to greedy, sampled and beam decoding alike.

\noindent\textbf{Formal verification.}
Both results are formalised in Lean~4 against \texttt{mathlib}. Part~(i)
specialises \texttt{mathlib}'s Banach fixed-point machinery; (ii)--(iv) and all of
Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} are proved from scratch. The development contains no
\texttt{sorry}, and an axiom audit confirms every exported theorem depends only
on \texttt{propext}, \texttt{Classical.choice} and \texttt{Quot.sound}. Beyond
assurance, formalisation forced the separation between what is proved (the
implication) and what is measured (the premise), and is why~\eqref{eq:horizon}
carries explicit constants rather than an asymptotic.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\noindent\textbf{Stimuli.}
A parametric repetition ladder of \NStimuli{} items: carrier sentences with a
target word repeated $k \in \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,32\}$ times, plus repeated
sentences, tongue twisters, and English number phrases with intrinsic digit-word
repetition. Crucially, every word- and sentence-repetition item at $k\ge2$ has a
\emph{length-matched control}: the same carrier and word count, with the repeated
token replaced by $k$ distinct fillers, isolating periodicity from length.

\noindent\textbf{Models.}
\NModels{} checkpoints spanning \NFamilies{} families: Llasa at 1B/3B/8B (Llama
backbones over X-codec2 tokens~\cite{ye2025llasa}), a within-architecture scale
ladder; XTTS-v2~\cite{casanova2024xtts}; and Qwen3-TTS at 0.6B/1.7B. Each item is
generated with \NSeeds{} seeds. A seventh run, XTTS-v2 with its shipped
repetition penalty disabled, is an ablation of a panel member and is reported
separately, never pooled.

\noindent\textbf{Behavioural measurement, and why the obvious judge is wrong.}
The natural instrument is Whisper large-v3~\cite{radford2023whisper}, and it is
demonstrably the wrong one here: its decoder is itself autoregressive with a
language-model prior, so it is subject to the very repetition-suppression
dynamics under study. Audited against concatenative audio with known ground
truth, its counted/true ratio falls to $0.27$--$0.65$ for $k\ge4$, while
\emph{same-voice distinct-word} sequences of identical length and silence
structure score $1.00$ at every $k$ up to $32$ --- a bias specific to
periodicity, pointing the same way as the effect we want to measure. We therefore
score with a CTC recogniser (\texttt{wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self}): no decoder,
no language model, output length governed by the acoustics. Worse in absolute
WER, right for this purpose. Both transcript sets are released.

The reported quantity is the \emph{relative count error} $(\hat c - k)/k$, where
$\hat c$ is how many of the $k$ requested units the transcript delivers.
Exact-match accuracy is the wrong resolution --- it scores $30$-of-$32$ and
$3$-of-$32$ alike and flips on $\pm1$ of recogniser slop --- whereas relative
error is signed, separating premature stopping from looping, and scale-free.
Audio-level degeneracy (silence, spectral flatness, clipping) is detected
separately and reported as its own rate.

\noindent\textbf{State measurement.}
For each instrumented generation we record per-step hidden states at probe layers
and head-averaged attention onto the text span. The statistic is the effective
rank of the generation trajectory, $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} =
\exp(-\sum_i p_i \log p_i)$ over normalised singular values, as a function of
$k$; Section~\ref{sec:negative} explains why we do not measure $q$ by
differencing boundary states.

\noindent\textbf{Code and data.}
The Lean development, the stimulus set, all generation and analysis code, and the
per-item result tables are released at
\url{https://github.com/lab260ru/icassp_antispoofing}. A single command
(\texttt{scripts/check\_lean.sh}) rebuilds the formal artifact and reprints the
axiom audit; \texttt{paper/build.sh} regenerates every number in this paper from
the released tables.
